title: Quick-commerce order tracker at 375 px
summary: Build the order-tracking screen for a fictional ten-minute grocery app: live status, an honest ETA, accessible, and still useful when the signal drops.
context: Pocketmart is a fictional grocery app that promises delivery in about ten minutes. After checkout the customer watches one screen, the order tracker, on a mid-range phone, on patchy 4G, in a lift, with one hand.

There is no backend to call. You write a small fake order feed (a script or mock endpoint) that moves an order through placed, packing, picked up, nearby and delivered, and sometimes adds a delay or an out-of-stock item. Build the screen against that feed.
Design for 375 px wide first. Desktop only has to not break.
must_have: A tracker screen with the current status as a clear step sequence, an ETA shown as a range that widens or narrows as the feed changes (never a falsely precise minute), and the rider's first name and a call button once the order is picked up.
Live updates from the feed (polling, server-sent events or a websocket) with a visible 'last updated' indicator.
Offline tolerance: when the connection drops, the last known state stays on screen, says it is stale, and recovers by itself when the connection returns.
Accessibility you can show: keyboard operable, status changes announced to a screen reader without spamming it, passing contrast, tap targets of at least 44 px, reduced motion respected.
nice_to_have: An out-of-stock flow: the customer chooses replace or remove for one item.
A map-free progress view for the last 500 metres.
Installable as a PWA, with the app shell cached.
constraints: No paid services, APIs or accounts. No map SDK that needs a key or a card; draw any map yourself or skip it.
Fictional data only: every name, address, item and rider is made up.
Any UI kit must be free; say which one and why.
deliverables: A public repo created after you press Start, with commits spread across the window.
A README with how to run the app and the fake feed, how to simulate a dropped connection, the accessibility checks you ran and what they found, and what is missing.
Two screenshots at 375 px in the repo: a normal state and an offline state.
judge_focus: Whether the ETA is honest when the feed is late, contradictory or silent.
What the offline state taught you about your state model, and the tests or checks that prove it.
Accessibility that was verified, not just listed as intentions.
A trail of commits: a working shell early, then the awkward states, with notes on what you dropped.
bengaluru_context: Consumer-product teams at Bengaluru quick-commerce and food-delivery companies build this screen, where a slow connection and a worried customer are the normal case.
